{
  q: "You are a project manager at a fintech company. Your team is building a new mobile payment feature. The designer has just submitted final mockups two days before the sprint ends but the developer says they need one more week to implement it properly. What do you do?",
  a: `This is a scope and timeline conflict that I have seen many times and the worst response is to pressure the developer to rush the implementation.\n\nThe first thing I do is understand specifically what the developer needs the extra week for. Is it genuine complexity in the implementation that was not visible from the mockups? Is it a dependency on another system that creates the delay? Or is it a capacity issue where the developer is working on other tasks simultaneously? Each of these has a different resolution.\n\nIf it is genuine implementation complexity, I go back to the designer and product owner with a specific question: which elements of the mockup are essential for the MVP and which are enhancements we can defer? A payment feature that works correctly with a simplified UI is better than a rushed implementation of a complex UI that has bugs. I look for a version of the feature that the developer can build correctly in the remaining two days.\n\nIf it is a capacity issue, I look at whether any other tasks can be temporarily deprioritized to give the developer the focus time they need on this specific feature.\n\nIf neither option works, I extend the sprint by one week for this specific feature rather than rushing a poor quality implementation into production. A payment feature with bugs in a fintech product creates customer trust issues and potential regulatory complaints that cost far more than a one week delay.\n\nI communicate the adjustment proactively to stakeholders with a clear reason, not an apology. Timeline adjustments for quality reasons in regulated financial products are responsible project management, not failure.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a bank. Your team is migrating customer data to a new system. On day three of the migration, a team member reports they made an error that corrupted 500 customer records. What is your immediate response?",
  a: `Stop the migration immediately. Do not let another record be processed until the scope of the corruption is understood.\n\nIn the first 30 minutes I need three things. A precise count of how many records are affected and which customers they belong to. A clear understanding of what the corruption actually looks like — are these records overwritten, deleted, or incorrectly transformed? And a confirmation from the technical team of whether we have a clean backup from before the error occurred.\n\nIf a clean backup exists, the recovery path is straightforward: restore the corrupted records from backup and reprocess them correctly after understanding what caused the original error. The timeline extends but the data integrity is recoverable.\n\nIf no clean backup exists, I escalate immediately to the project sponsor and the data governance team. 500 corrupted customer records at a bank is a potential regulatory notification event under RBI data protection guidelines and that decision is above my authority level.\n\nParallel to the technical recovery I work with the team member who made the error to understand precisely what happened. Not to assign blame but to understand the process gap that allowed the error to occur and ensure it cannot happen to the remaining records in the migration.\n\nI document everything from the moment the error was reported with timestamps. In a banking data migration, the audit trail of how an error was discovered, escalated, and resolved is as important as the resolution itself for any subsequent regulatory review.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at an insurance company. Your project has a weekly status report due to the senior leadership team every Friday. It is Thursday and you realize the report will show the project is two weeks behind schedule. What do you do?",
  a: `I send the report on Friday with the accurate status. I do not delay it, soften the numbers, or wait to see if things improve next week.\n\nLeadership finding out a project is two weeks behind on Friday from a status report is a significantly better outcome than leadership finding out three weeks later when the delay has grown to five weeks and they have been receiving inaccurate reports in the meantime. Trust is harder to rebuild than a schedule.\n\nThe report I send does three things. It states the delay clearly and specifically — we are two weeks behind the baseline schedule on the claims processing module integration. It explains the cause — the vendor API documentation was incomplete and our team spent eight days resolving integration errors that were not anticipated in the original plan. And it presents the recovery path — here are the three actions we are taking to compress the remaining schedule and here is our revised completion date.\n\nBefore I send the report I brief my direct manager verbally so they are not surprised by what they read. A manager who reads bad news for the first time in a written report that is also going to senior leadership is in a difficult position. Giving them advance notice is professional courtesy and gives them the opportunity to add context or support the narrative before the wider audience sees it.\n\nAfter sending the report I focus on the recovery actions, not on managing perceptions. The best response to a reported delay is demonstrable progress in the following week.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a telecom company. A vendor who is delivering a critical component for your network upgrade project tells you on a Monday morning that their lead engineer has resigned and the replacement will need two weeks to onboard. Your milestone is in three weeks. What do you do?",
  a: `Two weeks of onboarding with a three week milestone means the replacement engineer has one week to deliver what the original engineer was working on for months. That is not a realistic expectation and I do not pretend otherwise.\n\nMy first call is to the vendor's account manager with a direct question: what is the vendor's plan to protect the milestone given this departure? This is their problem to solve first. They have a contractual delivery obligation and the internal staffing change does not transfer that obligation to me. I want their proposed solution before I start adapting my project plan.\n\nIf the vendor proposes using the resigning engineer for a knowledge transfer period, even two to three days, that is valuable and I push for it specifically. A well-structured handover with the departing engineer is worth more than two weeks of a replacement engineer working without context.\n\nIn parallel I assess what can be done by my own team or other vendors to reduce the dependency on this specific deliverable. Is there any work that can be sequenced differently to give the vendor more time on their component without affecting the overall milestone? Are there any elements of the vendor deliverable that are genuinely critical for the milestone versus elements that could follow?\n\nI update my project risk register immediately and flag this to my project sponsor the same day. A key vendor staffing change three weeks from a milestone is a high probability schedule risk that leadership needs to know about as early as possible, not at the weekly status meeting.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a fintech startup. Your sprint review is tomorrow and two of the five user stories planned for this sprint are not complete. The team lead suggests marking them as 90% done in the report. How do you respond?",
  a: `I tell the team lead directly that we are not reporting incomplete stories as 90% done and I explain why.\n\nIn software delivery there is no meaningful concept of 90% done. A feature that is not complete is not delivering value to users regardless of how much work has been invested. Reporting it as 90% done creates a false impression of progress, makes the sprint review misleading for stakeholders, and hides the actual velocity of the team.\n\nThe accurate report for tomorrow's sprint review is: three of five user stories completed, two stories carried forward to the next sprint. That is honest and it gives stakeholders the information they need to make decisions about scope, timeline, and priorities.\n\nI also want to understand why the two stories were not completed. Was it scope underestimation, unexpected technical complexity, team capacity issues, or blocked dependencies? Understanding the root cause is more important than the reporting question because it tells me what to change in sprint planning to prevent the same outcome next sprint.\n\nI acknowledge to the team that not completing planned stories is uncomfortable to report. But a team that is honest about its velocity in sprint reviews builds trust with stakeholders and gets more realistic planning decisions as a result. A team that consistently reports optimistic completion percentages erodes stakeholder trust and eventually faces much harder conversations when the full picture becomes visible.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a bank implementing a new customer onboarding system. Two days before user acceptance testing begins, the compliance team sends a list of 12 new requirements they want included. What do you do?",
  a: `Twelve new requirements two days before UAT begins is a scope change that needs to be assessed formally, not absorbed quietly.\n\nThe first question I ask the compliance team is which of the 12 requirements are regulatory mandates with a specific legal basis and which are process improvements or best practices. In banking, the answer to that question is critical because genuinely mandatory compliance requirements cannot be deferred regardless of timeline impact, while process improvements can be sequenced after launch.\n\nFor the mandatory requirements, I work with the technical lead to assess the implementation effort for each one specifically. Some compliance requirements are configuration changes that take hours. Others require fundamental changes to data flows that could take weeks. I need that assessment before I can give the project sponsor an honest picture of the timeline impact.\n\nFor the non-mandatory requirements, I recommend formally deferring them to a post-launch phase with a specific committed timeline. I document this recommendation and the compliance team's acknowledgment in writing so there is no ambiguity later about what was agreed.\n\nI do not simply absorb all 12 requirements and extend the timeline without a formal change request. That approach makes future scope additions easier because it establishes that requirements can arrive at any point without consequence. A formal change control process for late requirements, even in an agile environment, protects both the project timeline and the team's capacity.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at an insurance company. Your project kickoff meeting is next Monday. Two of the five key stakeholders have declined the meeting invite without explanation. What do you do before the kickoff?",
  a: `I reach out to both stakeholders directly, not through another meeting invite.\n\nA declined kickoff invite without explanation usually means one of three things: a genuine scheduling conflict, a low perceived priority for the project, or a political issue where the stakeholder has concerns about the project that have not been surfaced yet. I need to understand which one before the kickoff happens.\n\nI send a brief direct message or make a quick call to each stakeholder. I tell them I noticed they could not make the kickoff and ask if there is a better time that works for them, or if there is something about the project I should know before we begin. That open-ended question surfaces any underlying concerns that might otherwise derail the project after launch.\n\nIf it is a scheduling conflict, I find an alternative slot that works for all five stakeholders and reschedule the kickoff. Starting a project without key stakeholder alignment at kickoff creates problems downstream that are much harder to fix than a one week delay at the start.\n\nIf it is a priority concern, I take that feedback seriously and assess whether the project scope, timing, or approach needs adjustment before I convene the group.\n\nIf it surfaces a political issue, I escalate to my project sponsor with a specific description of what I learned and a recommendation for how to address it before the kickoff. Proceeding with a kickoff meeting while key stakeholders have unresolved concerns is a setup for a difficult project regardless of how well the kickoff itself goes.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a telecom company. Your project budget tracker shows you have spent 60% of the budget but you are only 40% through the project timeline. What is your immediate concern and what do you do?",
  a: `The immediate concern is that at the current burn rate the project will exhaust the budget before completion. Specifically, if 60% of budget is spent at 40% progress, the implied cost to complete is 150% of the remaining budget, which means the project is tracking to cost 250% of the original estimate.\n\nBefore I escalate I want to understand whether the front-loading is by design or by accident. Some projects are legitimately front-loaded because the most expensive resources or activities are scheduled early. If the project plan explicitly showed higher spend in the first 40% of the timeline, the current tracking may be within expectations. I check the planned spend curve against actual spend to understand the variance.\n\nIf the variance is genuine and unplanned, I need to understand what is driving it. Is it scope that has expanded beyond the original estimate? Is it resource costs that are higher than planned? Is it rework from quality issues in the early phases? Each of these has a different resolution.\n\nI bring this to my project sponsor immediately with the specific numbers, the root cause analysis, and three options: reduce remaining scope to bring the project in on budget, request a budget increase with a specific justification, or restructure the remaining activities to reduce cost. I do not present the problem without options.\n\nI do not wait until the budget is exhausted to have this conversation. The earlier a budget overrun is surfaced, the more options the organization has to respond.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a fintech. Your project's key developer is going on medical leave for three weeks starting tomorrow. This developer owns the most complex module in the current sprint. What do you do?",
  a: `The first thing I do is wish the developer well and make it clear that project continuity is not their concern during their leave. That boundary matters both for their recovery and for the team's culture.\n\nBefore they leave tomorrow, I ask for a focused 60-minute knowledge transfer on the current state of the module. Not a comprehensive documentation exercise — that takes too long and puts pressure on someone who is unwell. A focused conversation on where the module is, what the next three steps are, and where the known complexities lie. If they can leave any notes or code comments, that is valuable. If they cannot, I work with what I have.\n\nI immediately assess the impact on the sprint. The complex module will almost certainly not be delivered on schedule and I update the sprint plan accordingly. I identify which other team members have the closest knowledge of the module and assign the work to the most capable available person, with the expectation of a slower pace than the original developer.\n\nI communicate the situation to stakeholders proactively. Not in a way that creates alarm but in a way that sets accurate expectations. A key developer is on medical leave, the complex module will be delayed by approximately two to three weeks, and here is how we are managing continuity.\n\nI also use this situation as a prompt to assess the project's key person risk more broadly. If one developer's three-week absence creates a significant project impact, the project has a concentration risk that needs to be addressed through knowledge sharing and cross-training in future sprints.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a bank. Your project steering committee meeting is in one hour and you just realized the project status deck you prepared contains a calculation error that overstates progress by 15%. What do you do?",
  a: `I correct the error before the meeting, even if it means presenting from an imperfect deck or presenting the numbers verbally without a polished slide.\n\nPresenting incorrect progress data to a steering committee, even accidentally, creates two problems. First, the committee makes decisions based on false information. Second, if the error is discovered later, it appears intentional even if it was not. The reputational damage from a discovered error is significantly worse than the discomfort of correcting it proactively.\n\nIn the next 45 minutes I fix the calculation, update the affected slides, and briefly review the corrected deck to make sure no other numbers are affected by the same error.\n\nIf there is not enough time to produce a clean corrected deck, I present verbally with a direct acknowledgment: I identified a calculation error in the materials this morning and want to give you the correct numbers before we discuss. The actual project completion is X%, not the Y% shown in the slides. I will circulate the corrected deck after this meeting.\n\nMost steering committee members respect a project manager who catches and corrects their own errors. What they do not respect is a project manager who presents numbers they know are wrong because fixing them was inconvenient.\n\nAfter the meeting I put a quality check step in my deck preparation process to prevent the same situation in future steering committee cycles.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at an insurance company deploying a new claims management system. Your go-live is in four weeks. The testing team has found 47 bugs, of which 8 are marked as critical. What do you do?",
  a: `Eight critical bugs four weeks from go-live is manageable but it requires immediate triage and a clear resolution plan for each one.\n\nI start with the 8 critical bugs. For each one I need three things from the technical team: what exactly does this bug do to the claims management process, what is the resolution approach, and how long will it take to fix and retest? In claims management specifically, a critical bug that causes incorrect claim calculations or incorrect payment processing is a different category of risk than one that causes a UI display error.\n\nBased on that assessment I divide the 8 critical bugs into two groups: those that must be resolved before go-live because they would cause actual harm to claimants or regulatory non-compliance, and those that are labeled critical but could be mitigated with a temporary workaround or process control during an initial limited launch.\n\nFor the 39 non-critical bugs I do the same triage. Some will be genuinely minor and can be deferred to post-launch patches. Others may compound into significant issues at volume even if they seem minor in testing.\n\nI present the steering committee with a go-live recommendation based on this triage: here are the bugs that must be resolved before go-live, here is the current resolution status for each, and here is my confidence level that they will be resolved within the four-week window. If the critical bugs cannot be resolved in time, I recommend a limited pilot launch to a controlled user group rather than full go-live, which reduces risk while maintaining momentum.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a telecom. You have just taken over a project that is already three months in. The previous project manager left suddenly. There is almost no documentation. What do you do in your first week?",
  a: `The first week is entirely about information gathering, not about making changes or demonstrating value through action.\n\nDay one I identify the three most critical stakeholders — typically the project sponsor, the technical lead, and the most senior business stakeholder — and schedule individual conversations with each of them within the first two days. My agenda for each conversation is simple: what is this project supposed to deliver, what is the current status as you understand it, and what are you most worried about right now?\n\nDay two and three I sit with the technical team and the business analyst if there is one. Not to direct them but to listen and observe. What are they working on? What decisions are pending? What dependencies are blocked? I take detailed notes and start building a picture of the actual project state.\n\nBy the end of day three I have enough information to create a basic project health assessment: what is the scope, what is done, what is remaining, and what are the top three risks. This does not need to be polished. It needs to be accurate enough to have an informed conversation with the project sponsor.\n\nDay four and five I focus on the most urgent gaps: does the project have a clear schedule with owners for remaining work, are there any imminent deadlines that require immediate action, and are there any decisions that have been delayed because there was no project manager to make them?\n\nI do not commit to timelines or scope in the first week. I commit to having a clear project baseline document ready by the end of week two that all stakeholders can align on.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a fintech. Your team's velocity has dropped 30% over the last three sprints with no obvious external cause. What do you investigate first?",
  a: `A 30% velocity drop over three consecutive sprints without an obvious external cause is almost always a people or process problem, not a technical one.\n\nI start by looking at what changed three sprints ago. Did the team composition change? Did someone join or leave? Did the nature of the work shift significantly — for example, from feature development to debt repayment or infrastructure work that does not show up clearly in story points? Did a new process or approval requirement get added that is consuming team capacity without showing up in the sprint metrics?\n\nIf nothing changed externally, I have one-on-one conversations with each team member. Not a team meeting where social dynamics suppress honest feedback. Individual conversations where I ask directly: what is making your work harder than it was three months ago? What are you spending time on that is not in the sprint plan?\n\nThe most common causes of sustained velocity decline that I have seen are: untracked meetings and interruptions that consume development time, technical debt that makes every new feature progressively harder to implement, unclear requirements that require multiple rounds of clarification before development can start, and team morale issues from personal or interpersonal factors that affect focus.\n\nI also check whether the velocity calculation itself is accurate. If story point estimation practices have changed and stories are being estimated more conservatively, the velocity drop may be a measurement artifact rather than a real productivity decline.\n\nI present my findings to the team in a retrospective format, not as a performance management conversation. The goal is to identify and remove the obstacles, not to hold people accountable for a metric.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a bank. A team member comes to you privately and says another team member has been submitting work they did not actually complete, claiming credit for a colleague's contributions. How do you handle this?",
  a: `I thank the team member for telling me and I treat what they shared as confidential for now. I do not act on a single account without understanding the full picture.\n\nMy first step is to look at what objective evidence exists. In a project environment, work is usually tracked through task management systems, code commits, document version histories, and meeting attendance records. Before I have any conversation with the person being accused, I want to understand whether the observable record supports or contradicts the concern that was raised.\n\nIf the objective evidence is inconclusive, I look for patterns. Is this a one-time incident or a pattern across multiple deliverables? Are there other team members who may have noticed the same behavior without saying anything?\n\nIf the evidence suggests the concern is valid, I have a private conversation with the person being accused. Not as an accusation — I describe what I have observed in the project records and ask them to walk me through their contributions to the work in question. Their response tells me a great deal.\n\nIf the behavior is confirmed, I address it directly as a project integrity issue. In banking projects, accurate attribution of work matters for accountability, risk management, and performance reviews. I document the conversation and the agreement on how work will be tracked and credited going forward.\n\nI follow up with the person who raised the concern to let them know the matter has been addressed without revealing specifics.   q: "You are a project manager at an insurance company. Your project scope document was approved three months ago. A business stakeholder now says the scope document does not reflect what they actually need. What do you do?",
  a: `The first question I ask is when the stakeholder realized the scope document did not reflect their needs. If they are raising this now for the first time, I want to understand what triggered the realization — a demo, a prototype, or a change in their business requirements.\n\nI do not immediately accept that the scope document is wrong. The scope document was reviewed and approved by stakeholders including this person or their representative three months ago. Before agreeing to change scope, I want to understand the specific gap between what the document says and what they say they need now.\n\nI schedule a working session with the stakeholder to go through the scope document section by section and identify precisely which elements are misaligned. This exercise often reveals that the misalignment is in interpretation rather than in actual requirements — the scope document says the right thing but the stakeholder is reading it differently than it was written.\n\nIf the misalignment is genuine and represents new requirements rather than a misunderstanding, I process it as a formal change request. I document what the original scope said, what the stakeholder now needs, the effort required to deliver the change, and the impact on timeline and budget. I present this to the project steering committee for a formal decision.\n\nWhat I do not do is absorb the new requirements into the existing project plan without a formal change process. Scope changes that are absorbed informally without timeline or budget adjustment are how projects fail quietly — the work expands but the deadline stays fixed.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a telecom company. You discover that two team members have been having a significant conflict that is affecting their ability to work together on a shared deliverable. The deliverable is due in one week. How do you manage this?",
  a: `One week from a shared deliverable is not the time for a team building exercise or a lengthy mediation process. It is the time for a direct, practical conversation focused on the work.\n\nI meet with each person separately for 20 minutes. I do not ask them to describe the conflict or explain their perspective on the other person. I ask each of them one question: what do you need from the other person in the next week to complete the deliverable on time? That question reorients the conversation from the interpersonal conflict to the work requirement.\n\nI then meet with both of them together. I do not revisit the history of the conflict. I present the deliverable requirements and the timeline and I ask each person to confirm their specific contributions and dependencies on the other person for the next seven days. I make the interdependencies explicit and visible.\n\nI increase my own involvement in the deliverable for the next week. Daily check-ins with each person, clear communication about what is expected, and early identification of any blockers. My increased presence is not about managing the conflict — it is about managing the deliverable risk created by the conflict.\n\nAfter the deliverable is complete I address the underlying conflict properly. That conversation, which may involve HR depending on the nature of the conflict, is more productive once the immediate deadline pressure is removed. But during the delivery week, the only conversation I have is about the work.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a fintech company. Your product owner is consistently unavailable for sprint planning and backlog grooming sessions, causing the team to proceed with unclear requirements. How do you address this?",
  a: `A product owner who is consistently unavailable for sprint planning and backlog grooming is creating a structural problem that affects every sprint, and addressing it requires a direct conversation rather than accommodating workarounds.\n\nI schedule a one-on-one with the product owner and name the pattern specifically. Over the last three sprints, we have had incomplete or unclear requirements at the start of development because backlog grooming was skipped or abbreviated. Here is the specific impact: two stories had to be reworked mid-sprint, one story was split after development started, and the team has been making assumptions that required correction. I present the evidence, not just the complaint.\n\nI ask the product owner directly what is preventing them from attending these sessions. Sometimes the answer is a genuine competing priority that can be resolved by rescheduling the ceremonies to a time that works better. Sometimes it is that the product owner does not understand the impact of their absence on the team's ability to deliver. Sometimes it is that they are overcommitted across multiple teams and need escalation support to protect this time.\n\nI also propose a practical adaptation. If the product owner cannot attend full backlog grooming sessions, can they provide written acceptance criteria for the top five stories at least two days before sprint planning? This reduces the ceremony dependency while preserving the clarity the team needs.\n\nIf the situation does not improve after this conversation, I escalate to the project sponsor. An unavailable product owner is a project risk that sits above the project manager's authority to resolve unilaterally.`,

  q: "You are a project manager at a bank. Your project is using a waterfall methodology. You are at the requirements phase and realize that two key business requirements directly contradict each other. What do you do?",
  a: `Two directly contradictory requirements at the requirements phase is actually the best time to find this problem. Finding it here is far better than finding it during development or testing.\n\nI document the contradiction precisely. Requirement A says X. Requirement B says Y. These cannot both be implemented because implementing one prevents implementing the other.   a: `A risk is something that might happen. An issue is something that has already happened.   a: `Earned value management is a technique for measuring project performance by comparing the planned value of work, the actual cost of work, and the earned value of work completed.   a: `Managing dependencies between multiple projects in a program requires visibility into what each project needs from others, when they need it, and what the consequence is if it is not delivered on time.\n\nThe foundation is a dependency register — a structured document that captures every dependency across projects: which project is the provider, which is the receiver, what specifically is being delivered, when it is needed, and what the impact is on the receiving project if the delivery is late.
